_readme: Keys below match your actual brainData.json region IDs exactly (frontal-l, hippocampus, amygdala, broca, wernicke, cerebellum). Extend by copying the pattern for any other region id in brainData.json.

disorders.name: Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder

dsm5.criteria_summary: Exposure to actual/threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence; intrusion symptoms; avoidance; negative alterations in cognition/mood; marked alterations in arousal/reactivity, lasting >1 month.

icd11.notes: ICD-11 requires only 3 symptom clusters vs DSM-5's broader 4-cluster model, and has a separate Complex PTSD diagnosis (6B41) that DSM-5 does not formally distinguish.

disorders.evidence_strength: strong — consistent hyperactivation on fMRI, lesion and stimulation studies

sociocultural_notes.presentation_variation: Somatic symptoms (headaches, fatigue, unexplained pain) are frequently the primary presenting complaint in South Asian, East Asian, and many African clinical settings, sometimes with underreporting of psychological symptoms due to stigma.

regional_examples.note: Trauma often disclosed through physical complaints first; family/community context shapes whether formal diagnosis is sought.
Community and religious frameworks often mediate help-seeking; local idioms of distress may not map cleanly onto DSM/ICD categories.
More direct psychological symptom reporting; higher rates of formal diagnosis-seeking relative to global average.

sociocultural_notes.caveat: Differences reflect variation in presentation, stigma, and healthcare access/reporting infrastructure — not differences in underlying prevalence.

disorders.name: Major Neurocognitive Disorder (Alzheimer's type)

dsm5.criteria_summary: Significant decline in one or more cognitive domains interfering with independence; insidious onset, gradual progression.

icd11.notes: ICD-11 requires both a mental/behavioral code and a neurological disease code, unlike DSM-5's single combined code.

disorders.evidence_strength: strong — well-established hippocampal atrophy on MRI, correlates with memory staging

sociocultural_notes.presentation_variation: Cognitive decline may be normalized as 'expected aging' in some cultural contexts, delaying diagnosis; family caregiving norms strongly affect when formal evaluation is sought.

regional_examples.note: Strong filial caregiving norms can delay institutional diagnosis.
Lower formal diagnosis rates linked to healthcare access rather than lower prevalence.

sociocultural_notes.caveat: Global prevalence comparisons are heavily confounded by diagnostic infrastructure and life-expectancy differences.

disorders.name: Major Depressive Disorder

dsm5.criteria_summary: ≥5 symptoms over 2 weeks including depressed mood or anhedonia, causing clinically significant distress/impairment.

icd11.notes: ICD-11 drops DSM-5's symptom-count checklist for a more holistic clinical description, with clearer single vs recurrent episode staging.

disorders.evidence_strength: moderate — reduced dlPFC activity/connectivity is a consistent but non-diagnostic finding

sociocultural_notes.presentation_variation: Affective language ('I feel sad/empty') dominates presentation in Western contexts; somatic language ('my heart is heavy') is more common in many Asian and African cultural contexts.

regional_examples.note: Historically higher somatic presentation in clinical settings; evolving with mental health literacy campaigns.
Distress often expressed through bodily and spiritual framing; community/faith leaders are frequent first contacts.
High mental health literacy correlates with earlier affective symptom disclosure.

sociocultural_notes.caveat: This concerns presentation and pathways to care, not biological variation in the disorder itself.

disorders.name: Personality Change Due to Another Medical Condition (frontal lobe / disinhibited type)

dsm5.criteria_summary: Persistent personality disturbance representing a change from baseline, judged a direct physiological consequence of a medical condition (e.g. TBI).

icd11.notes: ICD-11 codes this as 'Secondary personality change,' embedded in its broader 'secondary syndromes' framework rather than a standalone personality-disorder chapter.

disorders.evidence_strength: strong — classic lesion-behavior correlation (e.g. Phineas Gage pattern)

sociocultural_notes.presentation_variation: Family tolerance for behavioral change and access to neurorehabilitation strongly shape whether this is formally diagnosed vs managed informally at home.

regional_examples.note: Access to formal neuropsychological testing and rehab is more available, leading to earlier formal diagnosis.
Behavioral changes post-TBI may be attributed to injury generally without formal personality-change diagnosis.

sociocultural_notes.caveat: Diagnostic rate differences here largely reflect access to neuropsychological assessment, not differences in true incidence.

disorders.name: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)

dsm5.criteria_summary: Persistent pattern of inattention and/or hyperactivity-impulsivity interfering with functioning, with several symptoms present before age 12, across ≥2 settings.

icd11.notes: ICD-11 dropped the DSM-IV-era age-12 cutoff's strictness slightly and aligned more closely with DSM-5's current criteria than earlier ICD-10 did — the two systems are now fairly convergent for ADHD, unlike for many other disorders.

disorders.evidence_strength: moderate-strong — consistent findings of reduced dlPFC/striatal volume and altered fronto-striatal connectivity, though no single biomarker is diagnostic

sociocultural_notes.presentation_variation: Diagnosis rates vary dramatically by country — driven heavily by differing school systems' behavioral expectations, teacher referral patterns, and access to evaluation, not by true prevalence differences.

regional_examples.note: Among the highest diagnosis and stimulant-prescription rates globally, partly linked to structured school referral pathways.
Historically lower diagnosis rates, partly attributed to a differing psychodynamic clinical tradition alongside behavioral models.
Under-diagnosis is common due to limited pediatric mental health infrastructure, not lower true prevalence.

sociocultural_notes.caveat: Cross-country ADHD prevalence comparisons are among the most confounded in psychiatry — treat rate differences as largely artifactual, reflecting healthcare/educational systems rather than biology.

disorders.name: Autism Spectrum Disorder

dsm5.criteria_summary: Persistent deficits in social communication/interaction across contexts, plus restricted/repetitive behaviors or interests, present from early development.
specifiers: Severity levels 1–3, based on support needs

icd11.notes: ICD-11 merged what were previously separate ICD-10 categories (childhood autism, Asperger syndrome, atypical autism) into one spectrum diagnosis with severity qualifiers — mirroring DSM-5's 2013 shift away from subtypes, though ICD only made this change with ICD-11 in 2019/2022.

disorders.evidence_strength: moderate — no single brain region is 'the' autism region; frontal, temporal, and amygdala involvement is consistently reported but as part of distributed network differences, not focal damage

sociocultural_notes.presentation_variation: What counts as 'atypical' social communication is itself culturally shaped (eye contact norms, directness of speech, play styles), which affects both parent recognition and clinician diagnostic thresholds.

regional_examples.note: Earlier average diagnosis age and more standardized screening tools (e.g. routine pediatric ASD screening).
Later diagnosis is common, often not until school-entry behavioral difficulties emerge, due to limited early screening infrastructure.

regional_examples.region: Cultures with strong collectivist child-rearing norms
regional_examples.note: Some socially atypical behaviors may be reframed as shyness or family-specific temperament rather than flagged for evaluation.

sociocultural_notes.caveat: This region entry reflects a distributed network association, not a focal lesion — autism is not caused by frontal lobe damage; it's a neurodevelopmental difference involving many interconnected regions.

disorders.name: Behavioral variant Frontotemporal Dementia (bvFTD)

dsm5.code: 331.19 (G31.09) — coded as Major/Mild Neurocognitive Disorder Due to Frontotemporal Lobar Degeneration
dsm5.criteria_summary: Early, prominent behavioral disinhibition or apathy, loss of empathy, compulsive/ritualistic behavior, and executive dysfunction, with relatively preserved memory early on — the opposite early-symptom pattern from Alzheimer's.

icd11.notes: ICD-11 again uses dual coding (behavioral syndrome + frontotemporal lobar degeneration as the neurological cause), same structure as its Alzheimer's coding.

disorders.evidence_strength: strong — progressive frontal (and often anterior temporal) atrophy is well-documented on structural MRI, distinguishing it from Alzheimer's hippocampal-predominant pattern

sociocultural_notes.presentation_variation: Because early symptoms look like personality/behavior change rather than memory loss, bvFTD is frequently misdiagnosed as a primary psychiatric disorder (depression, bipolar disorder) or even relationship/marital conflict before neurological evaluation occurs — a pattern reported across many healthcare systems, not just lower-resource ones.

regional_examples.note: Average diagnostic delay is commonly reported as 3-4 years from symptom onset across multiple countries, largely due to the behavioral (not memory) presentation being missed as neurological.

sociocultural_notes.caveat: This diagnostic-delay pattern is more a feature of the disease's atypical early presentation than of any single country's healthcare system.

dsm5.code: 784.3 (R47.01) — coded as symptom/general medical condition, not a standalone DSM-5 entity
dsm5.criteria_summary: DSM-5 has no dedicated aphasia category; documented under Neurocognitive Disorder Due to Vascular Disease or as a medical symptom code.

icd11.notes: ICD-11 gives aphasia its own discrete symptom code in the neurology chapter — a useful contrast to DSM-5's broader neurocognitive framing.

sociocultural_notes.presentation_variation: Access to speech-language pathology varies hugely by country, directly affecting recovery trajectory and how long the deficit is documented as clinically significant.

regional_examples.note: Early, intensive speech-language therapy is standard, improving outcomes.
Limited access to speech-language pathology can leave the deficit under-treated regardless of rehabilitation potential.

sociocultural_notes.caveat: Outcome variation here reflects healthcare access, not differences in the underlying neurological deficit.

dsm5.criteria_summary: As with Broca's aphasia, documented under Neurocognitive Disorder Due to Vascular Disease or as a medical symptom code.

icd11.notes: Same discrete ICD-11 code as Broca's aphasia (MB4Y); ICD relies on clinical description to distinguish fluent vs non-fluent subtype.

sociocultural_notes.presentation_variation: Reduced insight (anosognosia) common in this presentation can affect family/caregiver interpretation of the patient's behavior across cultural contexts — sometimes mistaken for confusion or psychiatric illness rather than a language deficit.

regional_examples.note: Family members may misattribute fluent-but-meaningless speech to cognitive decline or mental illness rather than seeking aphasia-specific care.

sociocultural_notes.caveat: Community awareness of aphasia as a distinct condition (not 'confusion') meaningfully affects care-seeking speed.

disorders.name: Temporal Lobe Epilepsy (focal seizures with impaired awareness)

dsm5.code: Not a DSM-5 diagnosis — epilepsy is classified as a neurological condition; DSM-5 is used only if a co-occurring psychiatric condition (e.g. interictal mood/psychotic symptoms) meets separate criteria
dsm5.criteria_summary: DSM-5 deliberately excludes epilepsy itself, reflecting the broader principle that DSM covers mental disorders, not neurological disease — an important distinction for students to internalize early.

icd11.notes: ICD-11, as a general medical classification, codes epilepsy directly in its neurology chapter with detailed seizure-type subclassification — something DSM-5 has no equivalent for, reinforcing that ICD and DSM serve different scopes, not just different criteria for the same conditions.

disorders.evidence_strength: strong — mesial temporal sclerosis (often involving the hippocampus) is the most common identifiable structural cause of temporal lobe epilepsy

sociocultural_notes.presentation_variation: Epilepsy carries significant stigma in many cultural contexts, sometimes attributed to spiritual causes (possession, curses) rather than a neurological condition, which profoundly affects care-seeking, marriage prospects, and social inclusion.

regional_examples.region: Parts of Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia
regional_examples.note: Epilepsy-related stigma remains a documented barrier to treatment-seeking and social participation in some communities, alongside growing public health education efforts to counter it.

regional_examples.region: High-income countries with established epilepsy care
regional_examples.note: Better access to EEG/MRI and anti-seizure medication generally shortens the gap between seizure onset and diagnosis.

sociocultural_notes.caveat: Stigma patterns are shifting with public health education globally and vary enormously even within the same country — avoid treating any region as monolithic on this point.

disorders.name: Ataxia due to cerebellar disease

dsm5.criteria_summary: Relevant to DSM-5 only if secondary cognitive/behavioral sequelae meet Neurocognitive Disorder criteria.

icd11.notes: Coded cleanly as a neurological diagnosis in ICD-11 — illustrates that not every neurological presentation fits a DSM-5 mental-disorder framework.

disorders.evidence_strength: strong — classic ipsilateral motor coordination deficit pattern

sociocultural_notes.presentation_variation: Access to physical/occupational therapy and fall-prevention resources varies widely, affecting functional outcomes more than the underlying lesion severity.

regional_examples.note: Structured balance/vestibular rehab programs are standard.
Rehab access gaps can leave patients with higher fall risk and slower functional recovery.

sociocultural_notes.caveat: Outcome differences reflect rehabilitation access, not differences in cerebellar pathology itself.

disorders.name: Posterior Fossa Brain Tumor (e.g., medulloblastoma, pilocytic astrocytoma)

dsm5.code: Not a DSM-5 diagnosis — brain tumors are neuro-oncological conditions; DSM-5 applies only to secondary psychiatric/cognitive symptoms if criteria are separately met
dsm5.criteria_summary: As with epilepsy, DSM-5 has no tumor category; this reinforces the same core lesson — DSM-5 covers mental disorders, ICD-11 covers the full scope of medical/neurological disease.

icd11.code: 2A00.Y (Malignant neoplasm of brain) or 2E82 (Benign neoplasm of brain), depending on tumor type
icd11.notes: ICD-11's oncology chapter codes tumors by histology and behavior (malignant/benign), paired with the neurological deficit code if relevant — a good example of ICD-11 functioning as a general medical classification rather than a psychiatric one.

disorders.evidence_strength: strong — posterior fossa tumors are the most common pediatric brain tumor location, classically presenting with ataxia, headache, and signs of raised intracranial pressure

sociocultural_notes.presentation_variation: Access to pediatric neuro-oncology, MRI availability, and timely referral vary enormously by country, directly affecting how early these tumors are caught — this is one of the starkest global health disparities in neuropsychology-adjacent care.

regional_examples.region: High-income countries with pediatric neuro-oncology centers
regional_examples.note: Routine MRI access allows earlier detection, often before severe neurological deficits develop.
Limited MRI/CT access and fewer pediatric neurosurgical centers commonly mean later-stage presentation with more advanced symptoms at diagnosis.

sociocultural_notes.caveat: Survival outcome gaps for pediatric brain tumors between high- and low-resource settings are large and well-documented — a genuine health equity issue, not just a diagnostic curiosity.
